title: Recurrences: recursion tree, substitution, master method
summary: Given any T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n), say what it means, draw its tree, and produce its Θ runtime — by tree, by substitution, or by the master method — and know which one Poon wants.
sourceNote: Lecture 6 slides (updated Sep 9), Lecture 7 slides (Sep 14), HW 6, HW 7, CLRS 4.3–4.5.

blocks.md: **The question** In Lecture 5 you saw merge sort, and Poon argued it runs in O(n log n) with a picture: n−1 divisions, then O(n) of merging per level times log n levels. That argument works for merge sort. But what about an algorithm that splits into three pieces? Or four pieces each a third the size? Or does n² of work to combine? You'd need a new hand-wavy picture every time. Recurrences are the *general* tool: write one equation describing a single level of recursion, then solve it with a method that works for every shape.

That's the entire chapter: **(1)** write the equation, **(2)** solve it. Writing it is easy once you can read T(n) as a sentence. Solving it has three methods — the recursion tree (draw it), substitution (guess and prove), the master method (look it up in a three-case table). Poon teaches them in that order because each one explains the next.

blocks.body: **What Poon will ask** HW 6: draw the first three levels of a tree and fill in a table. HW 7: four recurrences, "give the Θ solution if the master method applies, state which case and show the conditions are met; if it doesn't apply, say why." On the midterm the three master cases are printed on the exam sheet; computing n^(log_b a), picking the case, and spotting when it fails are not.

sections.heading: Writing the recurrence for merge sort

blocks.md: Chapter 0 gave you T(n) as "steps to handle n things." A recurrence describes what happens in one call of the recursive function — not the whole recursion, just one level. Merge sort on n things does exactly three things: it splits (cheap, constant), it calls itself on two halves, and it merges the results (a pass over n things, so some constant k per element).

blocks.title: Lecture 6 slides 9–10. The +kn is the merge; Poon writes it as O(n) first, then as kn to keep a constant to track.
blocks.body:
mergeSort(a):                         T(n) =
  if a.length == 1: return a            T(1) = 1                  ← base case
  left  = mergeSort(first half)         T(n/2)
  right = mergeSort(second half)      + T(n/2)      = 2T(n/2)     ← two recursive calls
  return merge(left, right)           + kn                        ← merge: k steps per element

blocks.md: Why only one level? Because the recursion handles the rest — the same way a recursive function doesn't re-describe its inner calls. Poon asks this on slide 9 ("Recurrence relations only need to capture what happens on one level. Why?"). The answer: the T(n/2) terms *are* the deeper levels, by definition.

- T(n) = 3T(n/5) + 17 — "three subproblems of a fifth the size, plus 17 fixed steps."
- T(n) = 3T(n/5) + 4n — "three subproblems of a fifth the size, plus 4n steps."
- T(n) = T(n−1) + 1 — "one subproblem of size one less, plus one step." (A loop in disguise: that's n steps total.)
- T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) — same as merge sort with the constant hidden; Poon writes both.

blocks.prompt: Write the recurrence for binary search (Lecture 5 slide 9: check the middle, recurse on one half).
blocks.answer: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1: one subproblem of half size, plus a constant to compare the middle. (Solution: log n levels × constant = O(log n).)

sections.heading: Solving by hand for n = 8 — where n log n actually comes from

blocks.md: Before the three methods, do the dumbest possible thing once: pick n = 8 and compute T(8) by plugging numbers in. This is what a recurrence *is*. Everything after is a shortcut for this.

**Unrolling T(n) = 2T(n/2) + kn at n = 8**
1. `T(8) = 2·T(4) + 8k` Plug n = 8 into T(n) = 2T(n/2) + kn. T(8) needs T(4), which we don't know yet.
2. `T(4) = 2·T(2) + 4k` Plug n = 4. T(4) needs T(2).
3. `T(2) = 2·T(1) + 2k` Plug n = 2. T(2) needs T(1) — and T(1) is the base case.
4. `T(1) = 1` Now go back up. T(1) = 1 — one thing, one step.
5. `T(2) = 2·1 + 2k = 2 + 2k` T(2) = two T(1)s plus 2k of merging.
6. `T(4) = 2·(2 + 2k) + 4k = 4 + 8k` T(4) = two T(2)s plus 4k.
7. `T(8) = 2·(4 + 8k) + 8k = 8 + 24k` T(8) = 8 + 24k. Look at the 24k: it's 8k + 8k + 8k — one kn for each of the 3 levels of merging. That's n log n: 8 · log₂ 8 = 8 · 3 = 24. The recursion tree is this computation drawn as a picture.

Two things to take from that. First, the recursion bottoms out at T(1) — without a base case the chain never ends, which is why Poon insists on T(1) = 1. Second, the 24k is 3 × 8k: three levels of merging, each costing k×8. The number of levels was log₂ 8 = 3. That's n log n appearing from arithmetic, no theory. The recursion tree is the same computation, drawn.

Draw every call as a box. Under each box, draw the boxes it calls. Write each box's *own* work (the f(n) part — the merge) next to it. Then add up a whole row at a time, because every box in a row is the same size and does the same work. Total = sum of the rows.

**Merge sort's tree, one level at a time**
1. `n` Level 0: one call on n things. Its own work — the merge — is k·n. Under it hang two calls it makes.
2. `n / n/2 n/2` Level 1: two calls on n/2 each. Each merges n/2 things, cost k·n/2. Total at this level: 2 × k·n/2 = kn. Same as level 0.
3. `n / n/2 n/2 / n/4 n/4 n/4 n/4` Level 2: four calls on n/4. Four times k·n/4 = kn again. The pattern: more nodes, smaller each, same total.
4. `n / n/2 n/2 / n/4 n/4 n/4 n/4 / n/8 n/8 n/8 n/8 n/8 n/8 n/8 n/8` Level 3: eight calls on n/8. Still kn. Every level costs kn. So the total cost is kn × (number of levels).
5. `n / n/2 n/2 / n/4 n/4 n/4 n/4 / n/8 n/8 n/8 n/8 n/8 n/8 n/8 n/8` How many levels? Sizes go n, n/2, n/4, … until size 1. That's log₂ n halvings (Chapter 0), so log n + 1 levels including the root. Total ≈ kn · log n = O(n log n).

The row for level i is the one that matters, because it's true for every level at once. At level i there are 2ⁱ boxes (doubling each level — Chapter 0's picture), each of size n/2ⁱ (halving each level), each doing k times its size. Multiply: 2ⁱ · k · n/2ⁱ — the 2ⁱ cancels — = kn. Every row costs kn, no matter how deep.

blocks.title: Counting the depth
blocks.body:
The tree stops when a box has size 1. At level i the size is n/2ⁱ. At what level does that hit 1?

1. Set n/2ⁱ = 1.
2. Multiply both sides by 2ⁱ: n = 2ⁱ.
3. "2 to what power is n?" — that's log₂ n. So i = log₂ n is the last level.
4. Levels are numbered from 0, so there are log₂ n + 1 levels in total (Poon's little table: n=1 → 1 level, n=8 → 4 levels, n=16 → 5).

blocks.title: Lecture 6 slide 27. Drop the +1 and the constant k when you switch to Big-O.
blocks.body:
Total = (cost per level) × (number of levels)
      = kn × (log n + 1)
      = kn log n + kn
      = O(n log n)

blocks.md: **When the rows are NOT all equal**

Merge sort is the special case where every row costs the same. Change the numbers and the rows change size. Poon does two on slides 28–33, and they're the intuition behind the master method, so slow down here.

blocks.title: Three subproblems of half size
blocks.body:
Fill the row for level i.

1. Nodes: each box makes 3 children, so level i has 3ⁱ boxes (not 2ⁱ).
2. Size: each child is half the parent, so size at level i is still n/2ⁱ.
3. Work per node: k · n/2ⁱ.
4. Total at level i: 3ⁱ · k · n/2ⁱ = (3/2)ⁱ · kn.
5. (3/2)ⁱ grows with i: level 0 costs kn, level 1 costs 1.5kn, level 2 costs 2.25kn… The BOTTOM row is the biggest. The leaves dominate.
6. Depth is still log₂ n (sizes halve). Bottom row has 3^(log₂ n) = n^(log₂ 3) ≈ n^1.58 leaves, each O(1). Total is Θ(n^1.58).

blocks.title: Two subproblems of a third the size
blocks.body:
Fill the row for level i.

1. Nodes: 2ⁱ (each box makes 2 children).
2. Size: n/3ⁱ (each child is a third of the parent).
3. Work per node: k · n/3ⁱ. Total at level i: 2ⁱ · kn/3ⁱ = (2/3)ⁱ · kn.
4. (2/3)ⁱ shrinks: kn, then 0.67kn, then 0.44kn… The TOP row is the biggest. The root dominates.
5. Depth: sizes divide by 3, so n/3ⁱ = 1 → i = log₃ n → log₃ n + 1 levels (slide 32).
6. A shrinking geometric series adds up to a constant times its first term, so the total is Θ(kn) = Θ(n).

blocks.md: *(figure)* Row cost by level. Left: rows grow (leaves win — Case 1). Middle: rows equal (multiply by #levels — Case 2). Right: rows shrink (root wins — Case 3). This picture IS the master method.

blocks.prompt: HW 6 Problem 1: T(n) = 4T(n/3) + cn. How many subproblems, what size, what combine cost? Cost at the root and at levels 1 and 2?
blocks.answer: 4 subproblems of size n/3, combine cost cn. Root: cn. Level 1: 4 nodes × c·n/3 = (4/3)cn. Level 2: 16 nodes × c·n/9 = (16/9)cn. Rows grow (4/3 > 1) → leaves dominate. Level i: (4/3)ⁱ cn; depth log₃ n; total Θ(n^(log₃ 4)) ≈ Θ(n^1.26). (That's the 'QUITE hard' Problem 2 — it's just the growing case.)

sections.heading: Method 2 — Substitution (guess, then prove by induction)

blocks.md: **Why it exists** The tree gives you a strong guess but the hand-waving ("about kn per level") isn't a proof. Substitution is how you prove a guess is right. It's induction from Chapter 0: assume the formula works for smaller inputs, show it then works for n.

blocks.body: the solution. From the tree: T(n) = O(n log n), i.e. T(n) ≤ c·n log n for some c.
assume it's true for the smaller input the recurrence uses. Here that's n/2: T(n/2) ≤ c·(n/2)·log(n/2).
the assumption into the recurrence and simplify.
the result is ≤ c·n log n for some choice of c. If you can, the guess is confirmed.

blocks.title: Prove T(n) = 2T(n/2) + kn is O(n log n)
blocks.body:
Every line uses one fact from Chapter 0. I'll name which.

1. Guess: T(n) ≤ c·n log n.
2. Assume for n/2: T(n/2) ≤ c·(n/2)·log(n/2).
3. Substitute into T(n) = 2T(n/2) + kn:   T(n) ≤ 2·c·(n/2)·log(n/2) + kn.
4. Simplify 2·(n/2) = n:   T(n) ≤ c·n·log(n/2) + kn.
5. Log rule 1: log(n/2) = log n − 1:   T(n) ≤ c·n·(log n − 1) + kn.
6. Distribute:   T(n) ≤ c·n·log n − c·n + kn.
7. We need this ≤ c·n·log n. Subtract c·n·log n from both sides: need −cn + kn ≤ 0, i.e. kn ≤ cn, i.e. **c ≥ k**.
8. k is a constant (the merge's cost per element), so pick any c ≥ k. The inequality holds. QED: merge sort is O(n log n).

blocks.md: **The step people get stuck on** Step 7 feels like it appeared from nowhere. It didn't: after substituting, you have T(n) ≤ (what you wanted) − cn + kn. The leftover "− cn + kn" is the only thing standing between you and the guess. It's ≤ 0 exactly when c ≥ k. That's the entire proof — the algebra is just clearing the way to that one comparison.

blocks.prompt: Use substitution to check that T(n) = T(n/2) + 1 (binary search) is O(log n). Guess T(n) ≤ c·log n.
blocks.answer: Assume T(n/2) ≤ c·log(n/2) = c(log n − 1). Then T(n) ≤ c·log n − c + 1. Need ≤ c·log n: need −c + 1 ≤ 0, i.e. c ≥ 1. ✓ So T(n) = O(log n).

blocks.md: **Why it exists** Trees and substitution work but take a page each. Most recurrences you'll ever meet have the shape aT(n/b) + f(n), and for that shape someone did the tree once, in general, and wrote down the answer as three cases. You match your recurrence to the shape, do one comparison, and read off the answer. It's a lookup table with one calculation.

blocks.title: a ≥ 1, b > 1, f(n) positive. Merge sort: a = 2, b = 2, f(n) = n.
blocks.body:
T(n) = a·T(n/b) + f(n)
        │     │      └─ work done OUTSIDE the recursive calls (divide + combine)
        │     └─ each subproblem is 1/b the size
        └─ number of subproblems

blocks.md: Every case is a comparison between two things: **f(n)** — the work at the root — and **n^(log_b a)** — which, as the tree section showed, is the number of leaves, i.e. the work at the bottom (Lecture 7 slide 21: a^(log_b n) = n^(log_b a) = # leaves). Poon borrows CLRS's word *watershed* for n^(log_b a): a ridge line. If f is below it, water runs to the leaves (they dominate). If f is above it, water runs to the root. If f is exactly on it, every level is equal and you multiply by the number of levels.

rows: f(n) is polynomially SMALLER than n^(log_b a)
f(n) is the SAME as n^(log_b a)
f(n) is polynomially LARGER than n^(log_b a)

blocks.md: "Polynomially smaller" means the *exponents* differ by some fixed amount ε > 0: f(n) = O(n^(log_b a − ε)). n vs n² qualifies (ε = 1). n^1.9 vs n² qualifies (ε = 0.1). But n/log n vs n does NOT — they have the same exponent 1, and a log factor is not a polynomial gap. That's the trap on slide 28, and it's HW 7 Problem 4.

- Match the shape. Write a, b, f(n) explicitly.
- Compute the watershed n^(log_b a). (Chapter 0 table: log₂ 4 = 2, log₂ 8 = 3, log₃ 27 = 3, log₂ 1 = 0.)
- Compare f(n)'s exponent to the watershed's exponent. Smaller by a constant → Case 1. Equal → Case 2. Larger by a constant → Case 3.
- Case 3 only: check regularity — a·f(n/b) ≤ c·f(n) for some c < 1. (Plug n/b into f, multiply by a, confirm it's a fraction of f(n).)
- Write the answer with the case named.

**The three canonical examples, worked (Lecture 7 slides 13–17)**
1. `T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n` Example 1 (Lecture 7 slide 13). Start by matching the shape aT(n/b) + f(n).
2. `a = 4, b = 2, f(n) = n` Read off a (subproblems), b (shrink factor), f(n) (the non-recursive work).
3. `n^(log_b a) = n^(log₂ 4) = n²` Compute the watershed: log₂ 4 = 2, so n². (Chapter 0 if this stalls.)
4. `compare f(n) = n  vs  n²` Compare the work-outside-recursion f(n) to the watershed.
5. `n is polynomially smaller (n = n^(2−1), ε = 1) → Case 1` n¹ vs n²: the exponents differ by 1, a real polynomial gap. Case 1: the leaves dominate.
6. `T(n) = Θ(n²)` Case 1's answer is the watershed itself: Θ(n²).
7. `n² vs n² — the same → Case 2` Example 2 (slide 16). f(n) equals the watershed. Every level does the same work, and there are log n levels — so multiply by log n.
8. `T(n) = Θ(n² log n)` Case 2: Θ(watershed · log n) = Θ(n² log n).
9. `n³ vs n² — f is polynomially larger (ε = 1) → Case 3` Example 3 (slide 17). Now f is bigger than the watershed by a polynomial gap. The root's own work dominates.
10. `regularity: 4·(n/2)³ = 4n³/8 = n³/2 ≤ c·n³ with c = ½ < 1  ✓` Case 3 has an extra check: the work must shrink going down the tree. Plug n/2 into f, multiply by a, and see it's at most a fraction c < 1 of f(n). Here it's exactly half. ✓
11. `T(n) = Θ(n³)` Case 3's answer is f(n) itself: Θ(n³).

**Why the regularity check exists (slides 29–31)** Case 3 claims the root's work dominates everything below it. That's only true if the work actually shrinks as you go down — geometrically, by a constant factor per level. a·f(n/b) is the total work at the next level; c·f(n) with c < 1 says "strictly less than the level above." A weird f(n) that oscillates (his example: n²(2 + cos n)) can be polynomially larger and still fail this, so the shortcut isn't safe. For every polynomial f(n) = nᵖ you'll meet, regularity holds automatically: a·(n/b)ᵖ = (a/bᵖ)·nᵖ, and a/bᵖ < 1 is the same condition as Case 3 itself.
**When the master method does NOT apply**

blocks.body: T(n) = n·T(n/2) + n². The number of subproblems changes with n; the shape breaks.
T(n) = T(n−1) + 1. Subtracting, not dividing — not the shape. (It's a loop; solve by unrolling: n steps.)
T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n/log n. Watershed is n; f is smaller but only by a log factor. Falls between Case 1 and Case 2. Say "does not apply" — that's the graded answer.
f(n) = n²(2 + cos n): polynomially larger than the watershed but doesn't shrink steadily. Say "does not apply."

For T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n): compare f(n) to n^(log_b a). Polynomially smaller → Θ(n^(log_b a)). Equal → Θ(n^(log_b a) log n). Polynomially larger and regular → Θ(f(n)). Otherwise the theorem is silent.

sections.heading: HW 6 and HW 7, solved in full

blocks.md: These are the questions the midterm will look like. Cover the answers, try each, then compare.

blocks.title: HW 6 Problem 1 and the 'quite hard' Problem 2
blocks.body:
Draw the first 3 levels, then generalize to level i, count levels, and total.

1. Subproblems: 4. Size of each: n/3. Combine cost per node: c × its size.
2. Level 0: 1 node, size n, work cn. Total cn.
3. Level 1: 4 nodes, size n/3, work cn/3 each. Total 4cn/3.
4. Level 2: 16 nodes, size n/9, work cn/9 each. Total 16cn/9.
5. Level i: 4ⁱ nodes × c·n/3ⁱ = (4/3)ⁱ · cn.
6. Levels: size n/3ⁱ = 1 → i = log₃ n → log₃ n + 1 levels.
7. Total: cn · Σ (4/3)ⁱ for i = 0…log₃ n. Growing series → dominated by the last term ≈ cn·(4/3)^(log₃ n) = c·n^(log₃ 4). Answer Θ(n^(log₃ 4)) ≈ Θ(n^1.26). Cross-check with the master method: a=4, b=3, watershed n^1.26, f = n is smaller → Case 1 → same answer.

blocks.title: T(n) = 8T(n/2) + n²
blocks.body:
Master method with justification.

1. a = 8, b = 2, f(n) = n².
2. Watershed: n^(log₂ 8) = n³.
3. n² vs n³: exponent smaller by 1 (ε = 1). Case 1.
4. T(n) = Θ(n³).

blocks.title: T(n) = 7T(n/2) + n³
blocks.body:
Master method with justification.

1. a = 7, b = 2, f(n) = n³.
2. Watershed: n^(log₂ 7) ≈ n^2.81.
3. n³ vs n^2.81: exponent larger by ≈ 0.19 (ε = 0.19 > 0). Case 3.
4. Regularity: 7·(n/2)³ = 7n³/8 ≤ c·n³ with c = 7/8 < 1. ✓
5. T(n) = Θ(n³).

blocks.title: T(n) = 27T(n/3) + Θ(n³)
blocks.body:
Master method with justification.

1. a = 27, b = 3, f(n) = Θ(n³).
2. Watershed: n^(log₃ 27) = n³.
3. n³ vs n³: equal. Case 2.
4. T(n) = Θ(n³ log n).

blocks.title: T(n) = T(n/2) + log n
blocks.body:
Master method with justification.

1. a = 1, b = 2, f(n) = log n.
2. Watershed: n^(log₂ 1) = n⁰ = 1.
3. log n vs 1: log n is bigger, but is it *polynomially* bigger? That needs log n = Ω(n^ε) for some ε > 0. No — log n grows slower than every n^ε, no matter how tiny ε is.
4. So it's not Case 2 (not equal) and not Case 3 (gap isn't polynomial). **The master method does not apply.** State that.
5. (For your own curiosity: unrolling gives log n + log(n/2) + log(n/4) + … ≈ log n terms of size ≤ log n → Θ(log² n). Not required.)
blocks.answer: Does not apply — the gap between log n and 1 is not polynomial.

blocks.prompt: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n log n. Does the master method apply?
blocks.answer: Watershed n. f = n log n is larger than n but only by a log factor — not polynomially. Does not apply (the famous gap between Case 2 and 3). The tree gives Θ(n log² n).
a=3, b=3, watershed n^(log₃ 3) = n. f = n equal → Case 2 → Θ(n log n).
a=16, b=4, log₄ 16 = 2 → watershed n². f = n² equal → Case 2 → Θ(n² log n).
a=2, b=4, log₄ 2 = ½ → watershed n^½ = √n. f = √n equal → Case 2 → Θ(√n log n).
a=1, b=2, watershed n⁰ = 1. f = n polynomially larger (ε = 1) → Case 3. Regularity: 1·(n/2) = n/2 ≤ c·n with c = ½. ✓ Θ(n). (Rows shrink by half each level: n + n/2 + n/4 + … = 2n.)

blocks.prompt: Draw the level-i row for T(n) = 5T(n/2) + n² and say which case it is without the formula.
blocks.answer: 5ⁱ nodes × (n/2ⁱ)² = 5ⁱ · n²/4ⁱ = (5/4)ⁱ n². Rows grow (5/4 > 1) → leaves dominate → Case 1 → Θ(n^(log₂ 5)) ≈ Θ(n^2.32).

blocks.prompt: Explain in one sentence why every level of merge sort's tree costs the same.
blocks.answer: The number of nodes doubles each level while the work per node halves, and 2ⁱ · (kn/2ⁱ) = kn.

exercises.title: Write the recurrence from the code
exercises.prompt: Write T(n) for this function (base case included), then say what a, b, and f(n) are.
hints: Count three things at the current call: how many recursive calls, how big is each, and how much other work is done. That's a, n/b, and f(n).
The trap is missing the third call — it's a repeat of the first, but the computer runs it again. Count calls, not distinct subproblems.
The for loop runs hi − lo + 1 = n times. Everything else at this level is constant.
solution: Three recursive calls, each on half the input: a = 3, b = 2.
The loop does n work: f(n) = n (plus constants).
For later: n^(log₂3) ≈ n^1.58, and n is polynomially smaller, so master case 1 gives Θ(n^1.58).
exercises.why: Reading the recurrence off code is the whole game. Every 'why is this recursive function slow' investigation starts by writing T(n) — and a duplicated recursive call like the third one here is the single most common performance bug in recursive code (it's what makes naive Fibonacci exponential).

exercises.title: Fill the recursion-tree table
exercises.prompt: For T(n) = 2T(n/4) + n, fill Poon's table for levels 0, 1, 2, and general i (columns: nodes, size per node, work per node, total at level). How many levels? Which level dominates, and what is T(n)?
hints: Level 0 is one node of size n doing n work. Level 1: how many nodes (a), each of what size (n/b), each doing how much (f of that size)?
The most common error is the level total: it's nodes × work-per-node, and both change with i. Write it as a product first, then simplify. Here: 2ⁱ × n/4ⁱ.
2ⁱ/4ⁱ = (2/4)ⁱ = (1/2)ⁱ. The per-level total *shrinks* by half each level. When the series shrinks, the root dominates — the whole sum is at most 2 × the root.
solution: Level 0: 1 node, size n, work n, total n. Level 1: 2 nodes, size n/4, work n/4 each, total n/2. Level 2: 4 nodes, size n/16, work n/16, total n/4.
Levels: n/4ᵏ = 1 → k = log₄ n, so log₄ n + 1 levels.
Total = n(1 + ½ + ¼ + …) ≤ 2n. The root dominates: T(n) = Θ(n). (Master: n^(log₄2) = n^0.5, f = n is polynomially larger, case 3 → Θ(n). Same answer.)
exercises.why: The table is how you reason about any divide-and-conquer cost — including parallel programs, where 'work per level' becomes 'work per round of machines'. If the per-level series shrinks, the top dominates; if it grows, the leaves do. That instinct transfers far beyond sorting.

exercises.title: Master method, four in a row
exercises.prompt: Solve with the master method, stating a, b, the watershed n^(log_b a), the case, and the answer. If it doesn't apply, say why. (1) T(n) = 9T(n/3) + n. (2) T(n) = T(2n/3) + 1. (3) T(n) = 3T(n/4) + n log n. (4) T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n log n.
hints: For each: write a, b, f(n) first, then compute log_b a as 'b to what power gives a'. Only then compare f to the watershed.
Two traps: (2) has a = 1, so the watershed is n⁰ = 1 — people forget log_b 1 = 0. And (4) is the famous gap: n log n is bigger than n, but not *polynomially* bigger, so no case fits.
Case 3 needs the regularity check: a·f(n/b) ≤ c·f(n) with c < 1. Do it explicitly for (3).
solution: (1) a = 9, b = 3, watershed n^(log₃9) = n². f = n is polynomially smaller (ε = 1). Case 1 → Θ(n²).
(2) a = 1, b = 3/2, watershed n^(log₁.₅ 1) = n⁰ = 1. f = 1 = Θ(1) matches. Case 2 → Θ(log n). (Binary-search-like.)
(3) a = 3, b = 4, watershed n^(log₄3) ≈ n^0.79. f = n log n is polynomially larger (n log n ≥ n^(0.79+ε) for ε = 0.2). Regularity: 3·(n/4)log(n/4) ≤ (3/4)·n log n ✓ (c = 3/4). Case 3 → Θ(n log n).

(4) a = 2, b = 2, watershed n. f = n log n is larger than n but only by a log factor — not n^ε for any ε > 0. Falls in the gap between cases 2 and 3: **master method does not apply**. (Recursion tree gives Θ(n log² n), but 'does not apply' is the graded answer.)
exercises.why: The master method is the two-minute estimate engineers use before writing a divide-and-conquer algorithm at all — 'if I split in 3 and combine in linear time, is that worth it?' Knowing its blind spots (the log gap, non-constant a) is what stops you from applying a formula where it lies.
